hook_clip: My spec never said what to tell a customer whose bug was already reported.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: So can Claude replace Jira for bugs? The spec copies the part of Jira a small team uses for bugs. One list, with steps to reproduce, a severity and a priority. One owner per bug. A fixed path from New to Fixed. And a public form, so customers can report bugs too.

The core rule is that fixed has to mean fixed. The person who fixed a bug can't verify it. The reporter or QA has to. Every bug gets a fix target from its severity, twenty-four hours for a critical one. And duplicates point to one bug, so the people who reported it hear when it's fixed.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation. Reporting, triage and the bug's lifecycle. The board, the list, duplicates and export. Then notifications, the hourly job, the weekly summary and the public form. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.

Here's what it built. The board has five columns, from New to Fixed. Bug one oh four is a P1, overdue by twenty-five hours, with two reports. Theo fixed bug one oh seven, so he can't verify it. Lucy, who reported it, can, and the activity log shows it was reopened once. The list works out every open bug's target, due in or overdue by. The outbox logged the weekly summary for everyone on the team. And on a phone, the assignee sees bug one oh four, overdue by twenty-five hours.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all thirty-one checks passed, along with fifty-six automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed five places where Claude had to guess. When a customer's report was marked as a duplicate, my spec never said if they get an email. When two people took the same bug at once, the second one got the wrong message. And some refusals, like unassigning a bug with no assignee, had no message at all. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't production-ready. Production sign-in, real email sending, the hourly job on a real scheduler, the public form's rate limit behind a real proxy, and hosting were never tested. Check those yourself before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Jira's Free plan costs nothing for up to ten users, but everyone is an admin, email stops at a hundred a day, and customers can't report bugs without a paid plan. Standard, billed yearly, is nine hundred and fifty dollars a year for up to ten users. Build it if your bugs live in Slack, email and spreadsheets. Buy it if you plan sprints in Jira, or want your pull requests to update bugs.
Everything is in one file. The data model, twenty rules, the seed data, four phase prompts and thirty-one checks, with all five fixes included.
